case_info.scenario: A 67-year-old woman underwent an elective left external dacryocystorhinostomy to treat her symptomatic nasolacrimal duct obstruction. The procedure was completed successfully without any intraoperative complications. On the third postoperative day, the patient presented to the emergency department due to persistent cervicofacial swelling and ecchymoses of the left eyelids and left cheek, which had been present since the first postoperative day (Figure, A). On examination, visual acuity in both eyes was 20/30, which was slightly worse than her baseline of 20/25 bilaterally. The left pupil was noted to be mildly larger than the right (by 0.5 mm) in both dark and light, with no relative afferent pupillary defect observed. Intraocular pressure was elevated in the left eye (24 mm Hg, relative to 16 mm Hg in the right eye). Extraocular motility in both eyes was normal, though pain with extraocular movement was present (worse on the left). Crepitus was confirmed with palpation under the left eyelids and left cheek. Dilated fundus examination showed clear and quiet vitreous bilaterally. Slitlamp examination and globe position were within normal limits, and no signs of chemosis were present. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the patient’s head revealed extensive emphysema throughout the soft tissues of the face and neck (Figure, B). The globes, extraocular muscles, and optic nerves appeared normal.

options.A: Perform an emergency decompression via needle evacuation
options.B: Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly
options.C: Perform surgical exploration and possible debridement
options.D: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits and sinuses

case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

dialogue_history.text: I understand your concern about infection, but the presence of crepitus and extensive emphysema on CT points primarily to subcutaneous air rather than an active space infection. The elevated intraocular pressure and mild anisocoria are more likely secondary to the mechanical effects of the air tracking into the orbit, compressing venous outflow or the globe itself. A more conservative initial step would be to rule out a persistent communication, such as a leaking lacrimal sac anastomosis, and manage the intraocular pressure medically.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

1. Mental Demand

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   Definition:

   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

case_info.caption: A, Color photograph showing facial swelling and ecchymoses. B, Computed tomography coronal image (bottom left) and axial image of the head showing extensive surgical emphysema (indicated by the arrowheads) that is more prominent on the left side.
case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids. While most cases tend to be self-limiting in nature,3there are important exceptions to be aware of. The spread of air can involve the orbits,4-7which can raise the intraorbital pressure and pose immediate risk to the optic nerve, which requires emergency decompression when present.7In extreme scenarios, subcutaneous emphysema can extend to the chest wall, posing risk for airway compromise and tension pneumomediastinum.2Lastly, subcutaneous emphysema can mimic necrotizing fasciitis.1Surgical procedures introduce the risk for postoperative infection, with rates of cellulitis after external dacryocystorhinostomy estimated to be between 1.2% and 7.9% based on whether systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is used or not.8When cellulitis occurs, it introduces the potential for gas-producing organisms to spread rapidly and cause necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.9If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected based on fitting clinical symptoms and supporting investigations (ie, elevated white blood cell count, low serum sodium concentration, and positive cultures), treatment warrants aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and possible hyperbaric oxygen therapy.9,10 The patient returned for follow-up on the fifth postoperative day, where her emphysema was continuing to improve. The patient made a full recovery within 2 weeks and did not require further follow-up with ophthalmology. Unfortunately, the patient had an allergic reaction during her second postoperative week, suspected to be linked to the course of antibiotics prescribed, resulting in a return to the emergency department for management of her symptoms.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Consider empirical antibiotics and manage the patient’s symptoms expectantly Despite crepitation being noted under her left eyelids, an emergency decompression via needle evacuation (choice A) would not be the preferred next step because there were no immediate signs of orbital compartment syndrome (ie, reduced extraocular motility, warmth, proptosis, and relative afferent pupillary defect coupled with increased orbital pressure and decreased visual acuity). Surgical exploration for possible debridement (option C) would not be the preferred answer because the CT did not show signs of gas-forming bacteria (ie, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess formation). Magnetic resonance imaging (option D) would not be necessary as a next step as there was no indication to further characterize the emphysema, and the diagnosis was made clinically with supportive information from the CT scan. Further questioning after the CT revealed that the patient had chronic sinusitis, which she managed by blowing her nose. The patient explained that her swelling seemed to worsen after clearing her nose, suggesting that the emphysema was likely linked to her nose blowing. Given her persistent symptoms and pain with extraocular eye movement, however, the presence of an allergic and/or infectious component could not be fully ruled out. The patient commenced loratadine treatment to manage any allergic component contributing to her emphysema, as well as erythromycin and amoxicillin/clavulanate to manage any cellulitis component (option B). She was discharged home with instructions to use cold compresses and lubricating drops to manage her symptoms. Close follow-up was arranged, and instructions were provided to seek emergency medical care if she developed signs suggestive of an infection (ie, fever, warmth, erythema, or worsening pain). Subcutaneous emphysema is a rare but known complication associated with dacryocystorhinostomy.1-3The connection that is made between the nasal mucosa and the lacrimal sac creates a susceptibility for forced air to become trapped within the subcutaneous tissues. This likely occurs due to disruption in the mucosal barrier following the procedure, which can act as a one-way valve to trap air. It may also be more likely with more anterior bone removal creating a plane to the subcutaneous tissues of the eyelids.
